title: POC weekly sync — batching & concurrency tuning
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review throughput tuning tests. Discussed continuous batching behavior, concurrency targets, queue depth, KV cache warmup, and quantized model variant tradeoffs. Agreed next tuning steps and a 1-hour stress run with new queueing params; Redwood to share updated config and cost delta.
next_steps: Redwood: send updated pilot config with queueing and concurrency knobs by 2025-03-20
Atlas: run 1-hour stress test with 2M tokens workload and share logs by 2025-03-24
Schedule follow-up to review stress test (30 min) week of 2025-03-24
action_items: Ethan Cole | Share updated pilot config (concurrency, queueing, batching) | 2025-03-20
Maya Lin | Add KV cache warming script and example command | 2025-03-20
Sofia Martinez | Run 1-hour stress run with new config and upload perf CSV/logs | 2025-03-24
Raj Patel | Provide representative prompt set + token distribution CSV | 2025-03-20
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, let's get started. We've got about 45 minutes. Um, quick roll call...
[00:12] Tom (Atlas PM): Tom here. Raj and Sofia on my side.
[00:18] Ethan: Great. Maya from our side will drive the tuning notes.
[00:25] Maya (Redwood SE): Cool, hi. Quick recap from last week: you ran baseline with hosted default batching and saw about 320 rps at 120ms median, p95 around 420ms, p99 ~1.4s, is that right Raj?
[00:40] Raj (Customer): Yeah that's roughly it. There was some variance though, sometimes p99 spiked to 2.1s during bursts.
[00:48] Maya: Right. So we ran two changes: continuous batching enabled plus bumping concurrency from 16 -> 24, and an experimental queue depth policy. The idea was to increase amortization of kernels while keeping p95 under 500ms.
[01:05] Sofia (Customer): Quick question, when you say continuous batching, is that the same as the auto-batcher we saw in the demo? I heard it holds requests for up to 15ms to build batches?
[01:14] Maya: Yes, exactly. It trades off a little added scheduling latency for much higher throughput. In our run we set hold window to 12ms.
[01:20] Raj: We observed throughput jump to ~480 rps but median latency rose to 160ms and p99 was still wobbly at 1.1s. So good TPS gain but tail still a problem.
[01:33] Diego (CSM): That's consistent — continuous batching improves token throughput but doesn't always solve pathological tails caused by cold KV cache or long prompts.
[01:42] Tom: We also noticed some requests got queued for a long time when the system hit a sudden burst. Can you explain how queueing/backpressure should look?
[01:51] Maya: Sure. We added a per-shard queue length cap and a max_wait threshold that will route overflow to a fallback (smaller quantized variant) or return 429 depending on policy. For the test we used queue cap 512 and max_wait 250ms.
[02:05] Raj: There were a handful of 429s — maybe 7% during a 10-minute blast test. That was concerning.
[02:11] Maya: Right, that means our overflow policy was kicking in. Two levers: increase concurrency/replicas or lower the max_wait and enable graceful fallbacks to quantized model.
[02:22] Raj: The quantized variant had slightly lower quality — some hallucinations on rare prompts. We want to avoid that in production.
[02:30] Ethan: Tradeoff conversation — reduce p99 with more capacity vs accept some quality regressions with quantized fallback. What are your priorities?
[02:39] Tom: p99 is the big one. Users notice the long tails. Cost is important but secondary.
[02:44] Sofia: Security note — the atlas infra team needs the private deployment config for any dedicated run. For now the POC is on Redwood hosted, but we will later test dedicated.
[02:55] Maya: For KV cache warmup: we saw hit rate at start only ~12% then it climbed to 72% after 10 minutes. That cold-start is a big contributor to spikes. We provided a warmup script but it wasn't run in the baseline.
[03:08] Raj: We missed that, our test harness didn't call the warmup. We'll include it in next run.
[03:13] Maya: Good. Also, batching + KV: when the cache is cold batching can inadvertently delay a request behind a slow generation. We noted a few outliers where a single long prompt blocked a batch.
[03:24] Raj: Any configuration to isolate long prompts?
[03:27] Maya: Yes — prompt length routing. We can route prompts > 2k tokens to a separate pool or limit batch size for them. Another option: dynamic batching that bounds by latency target rather than batch size only.
[03:40] Tom: Nice. On cost — what was the delta when you ran 24 concurrency vs 16?
[03:45] Maya: Rough estimate: 24 concurrency increased GPU utilization by ~22%, giving 50% higher throughput for ~18% higher hourly cost. We can provide a precise cost projection.
[03:56] Diego: Also quantified that enabling continuous batching reduced per-token compute by ~12% in that workload due to better kernel fill.
[04:05] Raj: Ok so the plan we discussed last week — you were going to try a hybrid: concurrency 20, hold window 10ms, queue cap 768, max_wait 180ms, fallback disabled for now, KV warmup on. Did you try that?
[04:19] Maya: Yes. That hybrid gave 430 rps, median 140ms, p95 390ms, p99 880ms — better tails but still some spikes during synthetic bursts.
[04:30] Sofia: Any difference when we used quant int8 vs fp16?
[04:34] Maya: int8 dropped median latency a bit (~10ms) and upped throughput by ~8%, but quality drop on edge cases returned. We flagged the exact prompts that degraded.
[04:43] Raj: Can you share that prompt list?
[04:45] Maya: We'll include it in the report — the "edge prompts" CSV.
[04:50] Tom: How about autoscaling and burst capacity?
[04:53] Ethan: We can open burst capacity to your pilot; it'll auto-scale by adding ephemeral workers when queue depth exceeds threshold. That helps p99 but costs spike for the duration.
[05:03] Raj: We're OK with short bursts of cost if it reduces p99.
[05:07] Diego: Operationally, we recommend two immediate steps: 1) warmup KV before the run, 2) run a 1-hour stress test with the hybrid config plus burst enabled so we can profile sustained behavior.
[05:18] Maya: For the stress test we suggest workload: 2M tokens across 3600s, with Poisson arrival to simulate real burstiness, and keep logs at token and request granularity.
[05:29] Raj: We'll do that. Any other observability knobs we should enable?
[05:33] Maya: Turn on per-token latency buckets, batch size distribution tracing, and model output quality hooks (match with your eval harness) so we can correlate quality regressions with quantized fallbacks.
[05:44] Tom: One more operational question: how does the system handle partial responses when a worker drops? We've seen truncated outputs in prior stack tests.
[05:52] Maya: In hosted we have checkpointing of KV and we stream partials; if a worker fails we try automatic retry to another replica using last KV snapshot for that session — but for some very long sequences state can be lost, we log those as errors and count them. We're working on improving seamless failover.
[06:13] Raj: Ok. Let's confirm next steps and owners.
[06:16] Ethan: Summarize: Redwood to send updated config + cost delta; Maya to add warmup script; Atlas to run 1-hour stress test and share logs. Follow-up meeting scheduled week of 2025-03-24.
[06:29] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[06:34] Ethan: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[06:38] [END TRANSCRIPT]
